resources.title: Cell structures
resources.summary: An animal cell, a plant cell and a bacterium, each drawn and labelled with the parts the specification names, and a table of what each part does and which cells have it.

visual.alt: An animal cell drawn as a rounded blob, labelled nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes and cytoplasm, each label joined by a line to its part
A plant cell drawn as a rectangle with a thick cell wall, labelled cell wall, cell membrane, chloroplasts, nucleus, ribosomes, a large vacuole and mitochondria
A bacterial cell drawn as a capsule, labelled cell wall, cell membrane, chromosomal DNA as a loose loop, two small rings of plasmid DNA, ribosomes and a whip-like flagellum

blocks.title: What each part does
rows: holds the genetic material that controls the cell
controls what enters and leaves the cell
where most of the cell's chemical reactions happen
strengthens and supports the cell; cellulose in a plant
holds cell sap and keeps the cell firm
one loop of DNA, loose in the cytoplasm, not in a nucleus
small extra rings of genes, such as for resistance to an antibiotic
spins to move the bacterium along
blocks.note: Animal and plant cells are **eukaryotic**: their DNA is in a nucleus. Bacteria are **prokaryotic**: no nucleus, and much smaller.

applications.title: Antibiotics
applications.body: Many antibiotics work by attacking parts only bacteria have, such as the bacterial cell wall or bacterial ribosomes, which is why they can kill bacteria without harming your own cells.

applications.title: Genetic engineering
applications.body: Scientists put a human gene into a bacterial plasmid, and the bacteria then make the human protein. Most of the insulin used by people with diabetes is made this way.

resources.title: The heart and circulation
resources.summary: The heart's four chambers, the four major blood vessels and the valves, drawn as the double circulation, with the route the blood takes and why the walls differ in thickness.

visual.alt: The double circulation: the four chambers of the heart between the lungs above and the body below, with the vena cava and pulmonary artery carrying blue deoxygenated blood on the heart's right side and the pulmonary vein and aorta carrying red oxygenated blood on its left, valves between the atria and ventricles, and the left ventricle drawn with the thickest wall

blocks.title: The four vessels
blocks.note: **Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.** The pulmonary artery is the one artery with deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein the one vein with oxygenated blood.

blocks.body:
**The route.** Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. The blood passes through the heart **twice** on each lap: that is the **double circulation**.

**The walls.** Atria have thin walls: they only push blood into the ventricle below. The **left ventricle has the thickest wall**, because it pumps blood all round the body; the right ventricle pumps only to the lungs, close by.

**Cardiac output** is the volume pumped each minute: $\text{cardiac output} = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$. At rest, $70$ cm³ a beat $\times$ $72$ beats a minute is $5040$ cm³, about $5$ litres a minute.

applications.title: Taking your pulse
applications.body: Each beat you feel at your wrist is the surge of blood the left ventricle has just pushed into the aorta and on through your arteries.

applications.title: Training for sport
applications.body: Regular exercise makes the heart muscle stronger, so each beat pumps more blood. A trained athlete's resting heart rate can be below 50 beats a minute for the same cardiac output.

resources.title: Maths in biology
resources.summary: The calculations Biology asks for, each with what the letters mean: magnification, percentage change, rates, BMI, cardiac output, the inverse square law, Fick's law and energy transfer efficiency.
resources.statusNote: Edexcel gives no formula sheet for Biology: Ofqual's formula sheets are for Maths, Physics and Combined Science. A question may give an equation, but learn these.

items.name: Magnification
items.symbols: Both sizes in the same unit. 1 mm = 1000 μm.

items.name: Area of a clear zone (Biology only)
items.symbols: $r$ the radius of the zone round an antibiotic disc

items.name: Percentage change in mass
items.symbols: A gain is positive, a loss negative. Used in the osmosis practical.

items.name: Rate
items.symbols: Or $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$ when you time how long a reaction takes

items.name: Waist to hip ratio
items.symbols: Both in the same unit, so the ratio has none

items.name: Cardiac output
items.symbols: cm³ a minute, from cm³ a beat and beats a minute

items.name: Inverse square law
items.symbols: $d$ the distance from the lamp. Double it and the intensity is a quarter.

items.name: Fick's law (Biology only)
items.formula: $\text{rate of diffusion} \propto \dfrac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness of membrane}}$

items.name: Efficiency of energy transfer (Biology only)
items.formula: $\dfrac{\text{energy in the next level}}{\text{energy in the level before}} \times 100$

applications.title: Checking a microscope photo
applications.body: A red blood cell is about 8 μm across. If it measures 40 mm, which is 40 000 μm, in a photo, the magnification is $40\,000 \div 8 = 5000$ times.

applications.title: Doctors and BMI
applications.body: A person of 70 kg and 1.75 m has a BMI of $70 \div 1.75^2 \approx 22.9$, in the healthy range of 18.5 to 24.9 that doctors use.

resources.title: Core practicals
resources.summary: The eight core practicals in Edexcel Biology: what each investigates, what you change and what you measure. Two, marked B, are Biology only.

blocks.title: The eight core practicals
rows: the image size, to work out magnification; a labelled drawing
how long amylase takes to break down starch, tested with iodine
colour changes: iodine for starch, Benedict's for reducing sugars, biuret for protein, ethanol for fats
the percentage change in mass of potato pieces
the antibiotic, antiseptic or plant extract
the area of the clear zone round each disc
the oxygen given off, such as bubbles from pondweed
the temperature, with small organisms in a respirometer
how far a coloured drop moves in a set time
how many of each organism in quadrats
blocks.note: Questions on the written papers draw on these, so know the method, the variables to control and the hazards of each.

applications.title: Hospital labs
applications.body: Practical 5.18B is how a hospital finds which antibiotic will work on a patient's infection: discs of different antibiotics on a plate of the bacteria, and the widest clear zone wins.

applications.title: Conservation surveys
applications.body: Ecologists use quadrats and belt transects to measure how plants change from a woodland edge into a field, as practical 9.5 does across a school field.
